title: The Sealed Servants and the Countless Multitude
summary: Before the seventh seal, four angels hold back the winds of judgment while God's servants are sealed on their foreheads. John hears the number of the sealed, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel, and then sees a multitude no one can count from every nation, standing before the throne in white robes. An elder explains that they have come out of the great tribulation, washed in the blood of the Lamb, and will be sheltered and shepherded by God forever.
story: Chapter 6 ended with a question: when the great day of wrath comes, who is able to stand? Chapter 7 is the answer, set as a pause between the sixth and seventh seals. Before any further harm touches the earth, God marks his own. The chapter then looks ahead to the end of the story, showing the sealed people safe before the throne with every tear wiped away. It reassures the churches of chapters 2 and 3 that faithfulness under pressure is not wasted and that the Lamb will bring his people through. The seventh seal will be opened in chapter 8.
historical: Revelation's first hearers lived where public loyalty was displayed and tested. Slaves could be branded, soldiers were sometimes marked with a sign of their unit, and devotees of certain gods bore their sign. To be sealed on the forehead meant to belong to someone openly. For small congregations under social and economic pressure, the image told them that God had already marked them as his, whatever the empire might demand. The phrase “the great tribulation” recalls Daniel 12:1, a time of distress such as never was, and Jesus' words about great distress in Matthew 24:21. Preterists connect it with the sufferings of the first century, including the Jewish war of AD 66 to 70 and Roman persecutions; futurists with a final period of distress before Christ returns; idealists and many others with the whole span of the church's suffering, which the New Testament elsewhere treats as already under way (Acts 14:22; Revelation 1:9).
cultural:
The sealing comes from Ezekiel 9, where a man with a writing case marks the foreheads of those in Jerusalem who grieve over its sins, so that they are spared when judgment falls. Behind that stands the Passover, where blood on the doorposts marked the houses the destroyer would pass over (Exodus 12). The four winds held back recall Zechariah 6:5 and Daniel 7:2, where the winds of heaven stir up the great sea.

The list of tribes is unusual. Judah comes first, not Reuben the firstborn, presumably because the Messiah is the Lion of Judah (5:5). Dan is missing, and Ephraim is replaced by Joseph, while Levi, usually left out of tribal land lists, is included. No certain explanation exists; many note that Dan and Ephraim were linked with idolatry in Israel's history (Judges 18; 1 Kings 12:29-30). The white robes and palm branches recall the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived in booths and waved branches (Leviticus 23:40), and also victory celebrations. That is why verse 15 says God will spread his tabernacle over them. Verses 16 and 17 weave together Isaiah 49:10 and Isaiah 25:8.
literary: The chapter is built in two scenes, and the hinge between them repeats the pattern of chapter 5. There, John heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb. Here, he hears a number, 144,000 from Israel's tribes, and sees “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue”. Many interpreters take the two as one people described two ways: first as the true Israel ordered for battle (the tribal list resembles a military census, as in Numbers 1), then as the international throng the promise to Abraham always intended. The number itself, twelve times twelve times a thousand, is a figure of completeness. The chapter ends with a dialogue between John and an elder in the manner of Zechariah's visions, where an angel asks the prophet a question he cannot answer and then explains it.

outline.t: The winds held back until God's servants are sealed
A multitude from every nation worships God and the Lamb
Who they are: out of the great tribulation, sheltered and shepherded

doctrines.note: The multitude cry, “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb”. Salvation belongs to God and comes through the Lamb's blood; the redeemed have washed their robes in it, a paradox that makes the point that his death, not their record, makes them clean.

Whether the 144,000 are ethnic Israel or the whole people of God, the chapter ends with one people drawn from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue, the fulfillment of the promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham.

The last verses describe the end of hunger, thirst, scorching heat, and tears. The hope is not escape from bodily life but its healing, with God dwelling among his people and the Lamb as their shepherd.

words.note: Sphragizō, to seal, to mark with a seal as a sign of ownership and protection. Paul uses the same verb for the Holy Spirit's sealing of believers (Ephesians 1:13). Sealing here does not exempt God's people from suffering, since they come out of the great tribulation, but it guarantees that they belong to him through it.

Thlipsis, pressure, affliction, tribulation. The basic image is of being pressed or crushed. John already calls himself a partner in the tribulation (1:9), and Jesus warned Smyrna of it (2:10). Whether “the great tribulation” is a final future period or the church's ongoing experience is a key difference between interpretive schools.

Skēnoō, to pitch a tent, to dwell. God will spread his tabernacle over them, recalling the tent where he dwelt among Israel in the wilderness. John 1:14 uses the same verb for the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us.

Poimainō, to shepherd, to tend and rule a flock. The Lamb becomes the shepherd, a striking reversal. The same verb is used in 2:27 and 12:5 for ruling the nations with an iron scepter; the one shepherd both guards his people and governs the world.

christ: The Lamb is at the center of this chapter's hope. The multitude stand before the throne and before the Lamb, their robes are made white in his blood, and in the final verse he is the shepherd who leads them to springs of living water. Christ is both the sacrifice and the shepherd, the one who died for the flock and the one who guides it (compare John 10:11). The promises of Isaiah 25 and 49, of a feast where death is swallowed up and a shepherd who guides his people to water, are here fulfilled in him. The countless multitude from every nation shows what his death achieved: the promise to Abraham's family has become a people from the whole world.

hard.q: Who are the 144,000, and are they the same as the great multitude?
hard.a:
Christians read this in several ways. Many futurists, especially dispensationalists, take the 144,000 as a literal group of Jewish believers sealed during a future tribulation, distinct from the multitude of Gentile believers in verse 9. Others take them as Jewish Christians within the early church, set beside believers from the nations. A large number of interpreters across traditions read the 144,000 and the multitude as the same people seen two ways, the whole church pictured first as the true Israel arranged like an army, then as the countless crowd from all nations; they point to the hear-then-see pattern of chapter 5 and to the way the New Testament calls believers in Jesus Abraham's offspring (Galatians 3:29). The 144,000 appear again in 14:1-5, which is part of this discussion.

This is a second-order question on which faithful readers differ. The chapter's plain point stands on every reading: God knows and marks his own, and none of them is lost.

questions: God seals his servants before the winds are released. How does knowing you belong to God change the way you face uncertain times?
John heard a number and saw a crowd no one could count. How does the picture of a people from every nation challenge the way you picture the church?
Verse 17 promises that God will wipe away every tear. What griefs are you carrying that you most want him to wipe away?
